title: Chapter 1.  Geography — The Chota Nagpur Plateau & Mineral Wealth

blocks.content: Jharkhand's geography chapter is dominated by a single defining physiographic feature - the Chota Nagpur Plateau - which explains almost everything distinctive about the state: its forest cover, its tribal demographic profile, and above all its status as India's mineral storehouse. This is one of the highest-yield geography chapters of any Indian state, given how directly its minerals feed into national-level economic-geography questions.

Jharkhand lies in eastern India, carved out of southern Bihar in 2000 (Chapter 4), and is bordered by Bihar to the north, West Bengal to the east, Odisha to the south, and Chhattisgarh and Uttar Pradesh to the west - making it a landlocked state at the meeting point of five other states.

The state is physiographically dominated by the Chota Nagpur Plateau, an ancient, geologically stable block of Precambrian rock forming part of peninsular India's oldest landmass, distinguishing Jharkhand's geology sharply from the younger, alluvial Gangetic plains of neighbouring Bihar to its north.

The plateau is not a single flat tableland but a complex of smaller sub-plateaus and hill ranges at varying elevations, including the Ranchi Plateau (the largest and most prominent, at an average elevation of around 700 m, on which the state capital Ranchi itself sits), the Hazaribagh Plateau, and the Kodarma Plateau, separated by river valleys and low hill ranges.

cells: Bihar (north), West Bengal (east), Odisha (south), Chhattisgarh and Uttar Pradesh (west)
Chota Nagpur Plateau (ancient Precambrian rock, part of peninsular India's oldest landmass)
Ranchi Plateau (largest, ~700 m avg. elevation, houses the capital), Hazaribagh Plateau, Kodarma Plateau
Parasnath Hill (Parshvanath Hill), approx 1,365 m, in Giridih district - also Jharkhand's most important Jain pilgrimage site (Chapter 9)
Substantial - among the higher forest-cover percentages of Indian states, dominated by Sal (Shorea robusta) forests

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Parasnath Hill (approx 1,365 m, Giridih district) is Jharkhand's highest point AND its most important Jain pilgrimage site (Sammed Shikharji) - a frequently tested geography-cum-religion crossover fact.

cells: Rises in Chhotanagpur plateau (Latehar district), flows through Jharkhand's coal belt into West Bengal
'Sorrow of Bengal' historically (flood-prone); now regulated by the Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC) dam system; flows through Jharkhand's most industrialised coal/steel belt
Rises near Ranchi, flows through Jharkhand, West Bengal and Odisha to the Bay of Bengal
Named 'golden streak/line' for gold particles historically found in its sands; flows past Jamshedpur
Major tributaries feeding into the Son/Brahmani river systems respectively

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: The Damodar River was historically nicknamed 'the Sorrow of Bengal' due to catastrophic flooding - this issue was substantially addressed by the Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC), modelled explicitly on the USA's Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) and established in 1948, making it independent India's first major multi-purpose river valley project.

Jharkhand is frequently and accurately described as India's richest state in mineral resources, holding the largest reserves of several key minerals and hosting a disproportionate share of the country's mining and heavy-industry activity relative to its geographic size.

The state holds significant reserves of coal (particularly around the Jharia, Bokaro and Karanpura coalfields - Jharia being India's premier coking-coal reserve, essential for steel-making), iron ore (around Noamundi and the wider Singhbhum belt), copper (Singhbhum copper belt, India's most historically significant copper-mining region), mica, bauxite, uranium (Jaduguda, India's first and most significant uranium mining site), and limestone, among other minerals.

cells: India's premier coking-coal reserve, essential for steel production; also site of long-running underground coal-seam fires
Major iron-ore supply feeding Jamshedpur's steel industry (Chapter 7)
India's most historically significant copper-mining region, mined since ancient times
India's first and most significant uranium mine, operated by UCIL (Uranium Corporation of India Limited)
Koderma is historically one of India's leading mica-producing centres

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Jharia (Dhanbad district) = India's premier COKING coal reserve (vital for steel-making) - distinct from ordinary thermal coal reserves found more widely across India; Jaduguda = India's first uranium mine, operated by UCIL. Both are among the most frequently tested single-location mineral facts in Indian geography.

items: Jharkhand: approx 79,714 sq km; borders Bihar, West Bengal, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Uttar Pradesh; dominated by the Chota Nagpur Plateau.
Highest point: Parasnath Hill (~1,365 m, Giridih) - also the Jain pilgrimage site Sammed Shikharji.
Key rivers: Damodar ('Sorrow of Bengal', now DVC-regulated), Subarnarekha, North & South Koel, Barakar.
DVC (Damodar Valley Corporation, est. 1948) = independent India's first multi-purpose river valley project, modelled on the USA's TVA.
Jharkhand = India's richest mineral state: Jharia (coking coal), Noamundi/Singhbhum (iron ore), Singhbhum belt (copper), Jaduguda (uranium, India's first), Koderma (mica).
